The art of video editing is an intricate process that involves a multitude of
complex decisions made by professionals. This expertise is rooted in an in-depth
understanding of storytelling and the video itself, as well as access to high-end
editing tools. However, many individuals lack the necessary skills and experience
to effectively utilize video editing software, hindering their ability to create
impressive videos. To bridge this gap, our research focuses on developing an
artificial intelligence system capable of assisting both amateur and professional
editors. This requires a comprehensive understanding of video editing, including the
reasoning behind various techniques and their execution. To this end, we have
collected a substantial dataset of 1,000 pre-existing videos, paired with their
corresponding editing decisions, cut locations, and temporal attributes. Furthermore,
our dataset includes a detailed log of professional editors' decision-making
processes, encompassing their assessment of video segments, selection of cuts, and
application of effects. To facilitate the advancement of AI-based video editing
systems, we have established a suite of benchmarks that assess the performance of
this technology. These benchmarks encompass three primary tasks: cut prediction, effect
prediction, and decision log prediction. To the best of our knowledge, our dataset
and benchmarks represent a groundbreaking achievement in the field of video editing
research. This initiative holds the potential to empower a large number of
individuals, including content creators, by providing them with the tools and
expertise required to create high-quality videos. Moreover, our research has the
potential to unlock new avenues for the development of AI-based video editing
software, which could be utilized in conjunction with existing editing tools. To
further support the advancement of this technology, our dataset, benchmarks, and
logically coherent effects suite will be made available to the research community.

Temporal modeling in videos using large-scale datasets is hindered by the computational complexity of training long-horizon video models, which can be attributed to the substantial memory and storage needs for processing extensive video sequences. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a novel approach called Gradient Forward-Transmission (GF-T), which enables the training of large-scale temporal video models on datasets much larger than available memory. By leveraging a specialized data structure, GF-T optimizes gradient propagation through a pipeline of memory-efficient buffers, effectively increasing available memory without altering the training process. This allows models to be trained on datasets up to 512 times larger than the available memory, while only increasing storage requirements. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of GF-T in achieving state-of-the-art performance on several video modeling benchmarks. The traditional SPARQL query language, widely used for accessing and querying the vast amount of Linked Data available on the web, has been proven effective in retrieving information from various domains. However, it has a limitation in its inability to handle more complex visual queries, such as those involving spatial and temporal relationships. To address this, we propose VGStore, a new system that extends the capabilities of SPARQL to enable the querying of multimodal spatial-temporal visual queries, specifically by utilizing RDF Scene Graph (RDF-SG). RDF-SG is a graph-based representation that encodes spatial and temporal information of entities, allowing for the creation of more sophisticated queries. By integrating VGStore with RDF-SG, we demonstrate its potential to enhance the capabilities of existing SPARQL-based systems, such as VQAL and VOWL, in retrieving information from RDF-SG. Experimental results show that VGStore outperforms VQAL and VOWL in terms of efficiency, scalability, and usability. Deep learning techniques have achieved remarkable success in image segmentation tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to variations in the training data. This research introduces a novel neural network architecture designed to mitigate the impact of data fluctuations in medical image segmentation. By incorporating an additional output that predicts segmentation uncertainty, the network can refine its predictions and align them with the corresponding input image. This refinement process, achieved through a simple yet effective formula, significantly enhances the accuracy of segmentation. We have rigorously tested our method on two distinct datasets and observed a substantial improvement in performance compared to conventional deep learning approaches. Moreover, the experimental results indicate that our method is particularly effective in scenarios where data fluctuations are most pronounced. Overall, our findings suggest that leveraging data-specific uncertainty information can yield significant benefits in image segmentation tasks, especially when dealing with data sets exhibiting substantial variation. Gravitational-wave detectors are now collecting an increasing amount of data, with the most recent LIGO detectors storing over 6000 hours of signals from 2017 to 2020.  Analyzing such large datasets requires specialized tools, as they contain numerous low-level details that can be lost with basic reduction methods.  In order to efficiently analyze these data, researchers rely on specific tools that can handle the complexity of real-time data collection.  In this paper, we present OctApps, a collection of Octave functions designed for in-depth analysis of gravitational-wave data, specifically tailored for the advanced LIGO detectors.  These tools enable researchers to identify and study individual signals, including noise from specific channels and signal artifacts, as well as to analyze and recognize interference from aircraft and other moving objects near the detectors.  Furthermore, they can be used to generate visualizations of the data, including 2D and 3D representations of the signals collected from multiple detectors. This approach involves two primary components: a feature correlation module and a feature refinement module. The feature correlation module identifies the most relevant information across the entire dataset, while the feature refinement module utilizes the compressed global information to refine the local features. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on various computer vision tasks, achieving significant accuracy improvements and feature simplification. Notably, this approach can be applied to any type of feature learning problem without requiring any additional modifications. This paper introduces a novel approach called LitRec, a literature recommendation system designed to suggest relevant papers to authors based on their current research interests. By utilizing collaborative filtering and incorporating novel methods for identifying key phrases and recommending papers, LitRec aims to simplify the research process. An evaluation of the system using data from the arXiv repository reveals promising results, indicating that LitRec can effectively suggest around 20-30% more relevant papers than its baseline counterpart. Moreover, user feedback suggests that LitRec provides valuable recommendations that are likely to be useful to authors in their research. Furthermore, the framework is expanded to investigate polymorphism driven by conformational changes in single-molecule crystals, and the effects of intermolecular interactions on the presence of multiple phases are explored. Ultimately, the study provides a comprehensive understanding of polymorphism driven by conformations, and identifies areas for future research. Mobile services based on augmented reality are becoming increasingly popular, yet they demand high-quality and reliable connections. Unfortunately, wireless networks often experience service disruptions due to signal degradation, which can severely impact user experience. To address this issue, this study focuses on improving the performance of mobile augmented reality services by minimizing the effects of signal degradation. We develop a novel approach that integrates a predictive model with a decision-making algorithm to optimize signal quality and user experience. By using real-world data and simulation testing, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in reducing signal degradation and improving user experience. Specifically, our approach can enhance signal quality by 18.39% and increase user satisfaction by 4.91% compared to existing methods. Our findings have important implications for the development of reliable mobile augmented reality services. The code for this research is available on GitHub.

A novel approach for quantifying the left venticle in 2D echocardiography images involves employing a steerable pyramid decomposition-based feature extraction method. This method overcomes limitations in traditional edge detection techniques, particularly in echocardiographic images characterized by artifacts like speckle noise and non-uniform scaling, by leveraging the pyramid decomposition technique to isolate relevant features. Extracted features from this process are then applied in a regression model to determine left ventricular dimensions, with the model trained using a dataset of manually annotated images. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in accurately quantifying left ventricular dimensions in independent test cases, with a correlation coefficient of 0.882 in regards to end-diastolic diameter measurements, rivaling the performance of a leading existing method. Notably, the proposed approach exhibits improved generalizability and robustness in its results compared to its predecessor, with reduced sensitivity to specific imaging conditions. This method's utility is further illustrated through its successful application in left ventricular volume calculations, with estimated values aligning closely with established clinical standards. This breakthrough has the potential to facilitate the development of more accurate echocardiography-based assessment tools for left ventricular function. Cache side-channel attacks have been a significant threat to software security for years, and recent high-profile breaches involving the L1 cache have highlighted the need for more effective ways to detect and prevent cache-based vulnerabilities. We have developed a production software analysis tool called CacheQL that uses a unique method of measuring cache hits to track down and map out cache side-channel paths in real-time. The effectiveness of our approach was demonstrated in a case study involving the popular Spring Framework, where we successfully identified a previously unknown vulnerability that allowed for the extraction of a target object from the cache. The results show that our tool can quickly identify and locate cache side-channel paths, even in complex software, and provide detailed information about the cache hierarchy and alignment. By using this tool, developers can take a more proactive approach to identifying and fixing cache side-channel vulnerabilities in their software. The source code for CacheQL is publicly available. A recent discovery of a saddle-point structure in Krylov methods' iteration matrices has led to the development of a new method called constrained preconditioning. This approach involves modifying a reduced system with a constraint matrix, leading to the discovery of a novel category of preconditioned Krylov methods. Through numerical experiments, the authors demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods in solving systems arising from the regularized optimal mass transport problem. To avoid mode collapse in Generative Adversarial Networks, we've developed a novel training approach that incorporates a penalty term into the loss function. This term is based on the Hessian matrix of the discriminator, allowing us to control the level of mode collapse. We introduce a parameter, $\eta$, that controls the degree of mode collapse, with higher values resulting in reduced collapse. Our method is tested on the MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CelebA datasets, with the Hessian matrix's properties being used to determine optimal $\eta$ values for each dataset. Our experiments show that our approach outperforms baseline GAN methods, especially on the CelebA dataset, with the added benefit of $\eta$ allowing us to adjust the trade-off between mode diversity and training speed. This is particularly useful, as our approach is shown to be faster than prior methods, even achieving state-of-the-art performance on the CelebA dataset. Furthermore, we've developed a tool to measure mode diversity, making our approach more accessible and efficient for practitioners. This work is available as an open-source Python package. Our findings are further supported by a comprehensive review of mode collapse in GAN training, with a discussion of future research directions in the field. In various fields such as social and biological sciences, network data often consists of multiple interconnected layers.  Despite the importance of these multi-layer networks in real-world applications, very little research has focused on the challenges they present.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel algorithm called MultiSAGE, designed to make predictions across different network layers.  By leveraging the similarity between nodes in the same layer, MultiSAGE can accurately forecast inter-layer connections and has been found to outperform existing methods in a variety of case studies.  Our research demonstrates that MultiSAGE can effectively utilize network information to enhance the accuracy of cross-layer predictions and thus improve our understanding of complex multi-layer networks.  The code for this algorithm is available for public use.  We anticipate that this approach will greatly benefit researchers working with complex, multi-layer networks and contribute to a deeper understanding of the structure of these networks. Cubic spline interpolation is widely used in engineering fields due to its ability to provide accurate approximations for smooth functions. However, its effectiveness declines when dealing with functions that experience abrupt changes in value or derivatives. A new method of interpolation is proposed that relies on monotone cubic splines, allowing for more accurate approximations, including at points where the function exhibits significant jumps. Recent advancements in vision-text models like CLIP have led to significant performance gains in zero-shot image classification tasks. Nonetheless, adapting these models to novel domains has proven challenging due to the necessity for retraining the entire model, a process that is both time-consuming and computationally expensive. In this study, we propose the domain prompt approach to facilitate the seamless transfer of CLIP to new domains. By incorporating domain-specific prompts into the CLIP encoder, we can effectively adapt the model to the target domain without modifying the decoder or retraining the entire network. Moreover, we introduce the domain prompt training method, a novel approach that enables the self-supervised learning of optimal prompts within an autoencoding framework. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in adapting CLIP to the Food, Cooking, and Anime domains, yielding superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art domain adaptation techniques. This research introduces a novel hierarchical control approach for controlling the adaptive movement of legged robots. The high-level control unit uses a simplified model to estimate desired movement trajectories and tracks the robot's actual position and orientation. The low-level control, a dynamic path planner, uses real-time feedback from joint sensors and ground reaction force sensors to plan optimal movement paths in real-time. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this control architecture in enabling a quadruped robot to adaptively navigate various terrain including flat ground, stairs, and uneven ground with a payload. The proposed system's adaptability and robustness are highlighted through its ability to automatically adjust movement paths in response to changing conditions such as reduced joint torque and uneven ground without requiring additional training. These versions must be distinct from one another, while maintaining a connection to the original image, as defined by a particular measure of similarity. We propose a novel approach to constructing these attacks, centered around a clustering technique that groups images based on non-essential characteristics. By analyzing the structure of these clusters, we can develop a more effective method for generating adversarial instances, which can be tailored to exploit the weaknesses of a given classifier. We have tested this approach on a variety of image classification tasks and found it to be highly effective in creating high-quality adversarial instances that can be used to evaluate the robustness of a classifier. Neural networks have been modified to operate with spikes instead of traditional gradients, which could lead to substantial performance improvements and energy efficiency by leveraging spiking neural networks.  However, current spike-based training algorithms have limitations in their accuracy and speed of convergence, often relying on gradient estimation through integration over time.  In contrast, we present a novel approach called Spikemax, which employs a more direct and efficient method for loss estimation.  By using a maximum operator to approximate the loss, Spikemax can be trained with a single time step, eliminating the need for integration and significantly accelerating its convergence speed.  Furthermore, Spikemax can be combined with existing gradient-based training methods to achieve superior results, demonstrating its potential in real-world applications.  Our experiments show that Spikemax can achieve comparable performance to state-of-the-art gradient-based methods on MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets, while achieving a significant reduction in training time.  By integrating Spikemax into a neural network, we observed a substantial improvement in accuracy, with an enhancement of 2.1% and 1.3% on MNIST and CIFAR10 respectively, when compared to a baseline model.  Our results demonstrate that Spikemax can be a valuable addition to existing spike-based training techniques and has the potential to accelerate the development of efficient and accurate spiking neural networks. We introduce a groundbreaking early stop rule for Krylov method solvers used to solve linear systems, which can provide significant speed savings in Interior Point Methods applied to conic programs. This new rule is adaptable to different Krylov methods and offers a flexible approach to existing preconditioned solvers. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical experiments with Interior Point Methods on a convex quadratic optimization problem. Additionally, we describe a customized preconditioner based on this termination criterion and show its benefits through numerical results. This preconditioner shows potential to enhance the efficiency of Interior Point Methods applied to large-scale conic programs. A corresponding MATLAB implementation is provided to facilitate further research into the termination criterion. This criterion is also available in C and can be easily integrated into other solvers. This study introduces a novel steganography method called SABMIS that embeds a hidden message within a single grayscale image, $K+1$ color images, or a combination of grayscale and color images, without requiring access to target images in advance. This approach differs from other color image steganography methods by embedding the secret message in a grayscale image, followed by a secondary embedding in color images, minimizing the color modification of the host images. SABMIS incorporates a new, efficient, and sparse embedding strategy that reduces the computational cost of feature extraction and embedding. This approach leverages sparse representation to embed the secret message in the host image's least significant bits. Experimental results confirm the superiority of SABMIS in terms of PSNR performance and color changes compared to similar methods. In the context of high-dimensional statistics, we establish a novel framework for measuring the impact of disturbances on linear functionals and low-rank matrices. Our framework offers a unified approach to determining the optimal rates of disturbance for singular subspaces and their equivalents. By leveraging these disturbance bounds, we derive novel minimax rates for high-dimensional, sparse linear functional estimation under orthogonal and general parameterizations. Notably, our results reveal the critical role of the singular values in shaping these rates, particularly under orthogonal parameterizations. Furthermore, our framework enables us to quantify the optimal sample size for achieving adaptive confidence intervals under orthogonal sparse regression models. Notably, our findings demonstrate that traditional non-adaptive confidence intervals may fail to achieve the optimal sample size, while their adaptive counterparts may be insufficient under non-nested hypotheses, highlighting a critical limitation in current statistical practice. Consequently, our results underscore the importance of adaptive procedures in high-dimensional, sparse regression analysis. Theoretical developments are complemented by simulation-based evidence supporting the validity of our theoretical conclusions. In e-commerce, product page development is crucial for achieving high search engine rankings, yet creating tailored pages for numerous user queries and search terms is extremely resource-intensive. Given the vast number of product-related searches, manually crafting optimal pages for each specific term is not feasible. Consequently, many websites prioritize a limited set of high-traffic terms and neglect less common terms due to limited resources. This paper presents a novel approach utilizing Deep Neural Networks to generate product pages for less common search terms with the goal of increasing organic search traffic. Our proposed framework is composed of three primary stages: a query classification module, a content creation module, and a post-processing module. The initial stage categorizes search queries into distinct groups and generates content recommendations based on those categories. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional methods in terms of ranking accuracy and time efficiency. Implementing this framework resulted in a 7.2% increase in organic search traffic for a leading online fashion retailer, highlighting its practical applications in real-world settings. Our research contributes to the ongoing investigation of leveraging Deep Neural Networks to enhance e-commerce search engine rankings. This paper explores asymptotic properties of a Markovian coagulation model influenced by external source terms, focusing on scenarios where the equation lacks a stationary solution. A kinetic theory is employed to derive a maximum principle for the solutions, which in turn enables the development of extended asymptotic formulas for stationary solutions in the absence of the source terms. Finally, the research identifies potential avenues for extending its findings to a broader class of coagulation models, including coagulation models with diffusion. A related technical appendix is included to establish the regularity properties of a fundamental operator in the kinetic equation. This approach enables researchers to create tasks with varying levels of difficulty and architecture, grounded in real-world applications and systems. The rapid growth of deep learning technology has led to significant advancements in computer vision applications, particularly in surveillance systems that utilize facial and pedestrian images to identify individuals. However, the use of such systems raises serious ethical concerns, primarily due to the potential for unauthorized data collection. To address these issues, the concept of privacy protection through data anonymization has been proposed, which involves modifying sensitive data to prevent individual identification. This paper introduces PedAnonym, a novel data anonymization model for pedestrian images that utilizes a generative adversarial framework to create realistic and disorienting distortions while ensuring the preservation of privacy. PedAnonym's model consists of two primary components: a privacy network and a quality assessment network. The former is responsible for generating distorted images that are difficult to recognize, while the latter evaluates the level of privacy protection and image quality in real-time. To ensure the model's adaptability, the design incorporates a learnable threshold for image anonymization. Experimental results demonstrate PedAnonym's effectiveness in protecting pedestrian identities and generating high-quality images that are suitable for use in computer vision applications. Additionally, the model's performance was evaluated through a crowdsourced study, which revealed that PedAnonym's distorted images are indistinguishable from real images, while other anonymization methods failed to provide sufficient protection. Low-rank tensor regression is a crucial predictive task, especially in contexts like medical imaging, climate modeling, and social networks. However, low-rank tensor regression faces significant computational hurdles, especially in its standard form, which involves a data tensor of $D$ rank and a sample size of $n$. Specifically, the standard approach involves a computational complexity of $O(n^2D^{3/2}\log n)$ and a memory requirement of $O(nD)$. This limitation becomes even more pronounced in large-scale applications. In this research, we introduce a new approach to low-rank tensor regression that leverages the concept of sketching. Our proposed method, called ISLET, rapidly estimates regression coefficients in a time-efficient manner, achieving a computational complexity of $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2} n \log \log n)$ with an error margin of $\pm \epsilon$. ISLET also boasts a memory efficiency of $O(n)$, which is significantly lower than the standard approach. Moreover, ISLET's sketching-based design allows it to be parallelizable, making it an effective tool for large-scale applications. Experimental results demonstrate ISLET's superiority over the standard approach in terms of both efficiency and accuracy. Additionally, we extend our method to address a related problem in low-rank tensor regression, which is the estimation of the residual variance-covariance matrix. Our proposed method, called ISLET-RVC, achieves a comparable computational efficiency of $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2} n \log \log n)$. The code for ISLET and ISLET-RVC is publicly available on GitHub. In graph theory, finding the vertex cover is a concept where a vertex cover is defined as a set of vertices that connect to at least one edge each. The goal in solving the vertex cover problem is to find the minimum possible vertex cover size. The problem of vertex cover is known to be NP-hard and difficult to solve exactly in polynomial time. To address this challenge, a new heuristic method called Circular and Bipartite Approximation Method (CBA) is proposed. This approach involves two main steps: first, finding a vertex cover in a related bipartite graph, and then using the solution to obtain a vertex cover for the original graph. Experimental results show that the CBA method performs well compared to existing approximation algorithms for vertex cover. To further enhance the CBA method, a new technique called Local Search (LS) is introduced, which involves iteratively applying local moves to find a better vertex cover. The effectiveness of the CBA method with LS is demonstrated through extensive experiments on a range of real-world graphs, resulting in improved performance compared to existing approximation algorithms for vertex cover. This paper delves into the structural analysis of market networks, a concept where relationships between economic agents are reinterpreted as electrical connections within a network. We propose a novel approach to analyzing this network by applying a dual interpretation, in which market participants are either viewed as buyers or sellers, generating two separate networks. Our method involves quantifying the flow of information between these networks using transfer entropy and comparing the resulting electrical circuit configurations. To achieve this, we develop a system for automatically extracting market participants, defining electrical connections, and calculating information flow. Our framework is applied to the cryptocurrency market, a highly liquid market network comprising 1000+ participants. The results of our analysis reveal a network characterized by a high level of symmetry and a transfer entropy that highlights the exchange of information between connected participants. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the market network exhibits a high degree of regularity, with most cryptocurrency participants acting as sellers and engaging in market-making activities. The market's network structure is also found to be sensitive to market fluctuations, with market downturns resulting in increased connectivity and market upswings resulting in decreased connectivity. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to detect market trends, predict price movements, and identify market turning points. The market network's structure is also found to be influenced by market liquidity, with increased liquidity leading to reduced connectivity and decreased liquidity leading to increased connectivity. The implications of our research are significant, as they suggest the potential for a deeper understanding of market dynamics and the emergence of market-making activities. This research has the potential to contribute to the advancement of market analysis and the development of more effective market prediction tools. The task of link forecasting aims to predict the evolution of graph connections over time.  Historically, this field has been viewed as a classification problem where potential future links are identified from a predefined set.  However, this approach has significant limitations due to the finite number of possible links and the lack of consideration for link characteristics.  To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel approach called Generalized Connection Learning with Semantic Correlation Recognition (GCLSCR), which integrates link forecasting with meta-learning.  By leveraging existing data, GCLSCR can predict future links and their underlying features, such as semantic contexts.  The method utilizes a two-stage approach that involves predicting future link features and then utilizing these features to identify relevant links.  The proposed GCLSCR approach is evaluated on real-world datasets and demonstrates its effectiveness in predicting future links and their associated features.  The results show that GCLSCR outperforms existing methods in terms of link prediction accuracy and the ability to identify semantic contexts.  An additional analysis of the predicted link features was conducted to assess their quality and usefulness for link prediction.  The code for the proposed GCLSCR approach is available on GitHub. This study examines the efficacy of using differential privacy in conjunction with standard regularization techniques on machine learning model training. By analyzing the trade-offs between optimization accuracy, data privacy, and model overfitting, we investigate whether optimizing a different loss function that is optimized in conjunction with differential privacy can achieve a balance between these competing demands. Our analysis reveals that as the degree of differential privacy increases, the choice of loss function becomes increasingly critical in determining the effectiveness of optimization. Through a combination of theoretical and empirical investigations, we have found that optimizing with differential privacy can yield significant improvements over traditional regularization techniques, particularly in settings where the data distribution is complex and the degree of differential privacy is moderate. However, in scenarios where the degree of differential privacy is high or the data distribution is simple, the benefits of using differential privacy in conjunction with standard regularization techniques are limited. Our findings suggest that future research on optimization techniques for training machine learning models with differential privacy should focus on developing new optimization strategies that are tailored to specific settings of differential privacy and data distribution. The search for higgsino particles at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is complicated by a significant background from top-quark production combined with a bottom-quark. Typically, this background is suppressed by analyzing the distribution of the longitudinal component of the lightest neutral higgsino's decay products. However, this approach is hindered by limitations in the detector's ability to measure the longitudinal polarization and by the particles' flight distances. In this research, we explore an alternative method that focuses on the angular relationships between visible and invisible particles in the decay process. Specifically, we examine the connections between visible particles and the invisible particle's direction, as well as between visible particles among themselves. Our findings indicate that these angular relationships hold considerable promise for reducing background noise while maintaining signal integrity. Furthermore, we propose a set of multi-variable cuts that achieve a substantial reduction in background noise with minimal impact on signal detection. In particular, this approach results in a 40% reduction in background noise while the signal remains unchanged, specifically for the higgsino particle with a mass of 150 GeV. Additionally, for the scenario where the mass of the higgsino particle is 200 GeV, the background noise can be reduced by 60% while the signal remains unaffected. This research provides a foundation for further investigation into the use of angular analysis in the detection of higgsino particles at the LHC. In speaker authentication, standardized Mel-frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) features are typically computed using fixed, non-adaptive parameters. This paper presents a new method where the speaker estimation and acoustic modeling components within a speaker verification or identification system learn MFCC features jointly through a self-supervised process. This is achieved by incorporating a speaker estimation model that directly calculates d-vector embeddings, which are subsequently used to train an MFCC extractor. This process involves training an MFCC extractor to transform short-time windowed audio into d-vector embeddings, which are computed using a speaker estimation model. This allows the entire system to be trained end-to-end without relying on traditional cepstral extraction algorithms. This approach is referred to as trainable MFCCs (T-MFCCs). Experiments conducted on the VoxCeleb dataset for speaker verification and on the VoxCeleb and SITW datasets for speaker identification demonstrate that T-MFCCs achieve comparable performance to baseline algorithms using Sinc-based MFCCs. Notably, the T-MFCC method also exhibits improved computational efficiency, with a 50% reduction in processing time. This is attributed to the fact that T-MFCCs eliminate the need for the traditional MFCC extraction process. This work is anticipated to contribute to the development of more efficient and scalable speaker systems in the future. In a related study, Joudrey and Roeloffs (2020) introduced the False Discovery Ratio (FDR) and its estimation for a one-tailed t-test with a small sample size in independent scenarios. This paper extends their work to a correlated setting by analyzing the statistical behavior of the adjusted p-values under a finite sample size. It is demonstrated that the adjusted p-values conform to a multivariate beta distribution, enabling the derivation of the asymptotic behavior of the false discovery rate (FDR) and the False Discovery Ambiguity (FAD). The proposed methods are validated through simulations and empirical data analysis. Furthermore, the study examines the asymptotic behavior of the adjusted p-values when testing multiple hypotheses under a weak signal, revealing that the False Discovery Ambiguity can be mitigated with a sufficiently large number of tests. The findings are also compared with existing methods in related work. In conclusion, the study highlights the importance of considering dependence in statistical analysis to improve the accuracy of FDR estimation. This paper introduces a novel meta-filter technique to facilitate few-example learning by leveraging a minimal number of annotated dynamic videos to update a pre-existing static model. The core idea revolves around dynamic feature alignment, which is inherently difficult to achieve due to the continuous evolution of dynamic characteristics over time. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach called Meta-Filter, which utilizes a dynamic model to generate adaptive features for the static model. The Meta-filter method comprises three key components: a dynamic feature generator, a feature selector, and a model updator. The dynamic feature generator utilizes a meta-filter to produce dynamic features that are closely related to the input video. The feature selector employs a meta-filter to select the most relevant features from the static model, ensuring alignment with the dynamic features. Finally, the model updator integrates the selected features into the pre-existing model, enabling it to adapt to the new data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the activity recognition task, achieving state-of-the-art results on the UCF-HS and UCF-Crime datasets. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/MCG-NJU/Meta-Filter. Medical image analysis heavily relies on the application of deep learning techniques. 
Despite their effectiveness, deep neural networks struggle when applied to new domains without sufficient training data. 
To overcome this limitation, we propose an unsupervised domain transfer approach that utilizes feature disentanglement and GCNs for medical image classification. 
Our method first employs a Generative Adversarial Network to generate target domain images from the source domain. 
It then utilizes a feature disentanglement network to separate domain-invariant features from the generated images. 
Additionally, we incorporate a GCN to capture the domain-specific relationships between the source and target domains. 
Our proposed approach was evaluated on two medical image datasets, demonstrating superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods. 
The experimental results show that our method achieves an accuracy of 92.5% on the ChestX competition dataset and 96.5% on the NIH Chest CT dataset. 
Our findings indicate that domain adaptation with feature disentanglement and GCNs can effectively transfer knowledge from the source to the target domain without relying on labeled target data. 
Our approach can be effectively applied to various medical image classification tasks. 
Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the method's effectiveness and identify potential areas for future research. 
Our source code and pre-trained models are publicly available for download at the specified GitHub repository. 
Our work is expected to contribute to the advancement of medical image analysis and improve the accuracy of medical image classification.

A novel numerical approach has been developed to tackle a key challenge in computational neuroscience: accurately modeling neural activation dynamics through moment methods. The complexity of neural networks, characterized by numerous excitatory and inhibitory connections, makes traditional numerical methods (like finite differences and finite volumes) impractical due to high memory requirements. Our proposed method leverages the fact that neural activity dynamics can be represented using polynomial curves and splines to efficiently solve the neural activity equation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on a simplified model, the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, and compare its performance to traditional numerical methods. The proposed method offers significant advantages, including the ability to scale to large networks, be easily parallelized, and achieve accuracy comparable to traditional methods. Our results show that the new approach can achieve similar accuracy as traditional numerical methods, with a significant reduction in computational complexity. For instance, in a 1000x1000 neuron network, the method requires approximately 1 million floating point operations per neuron update, a substantial improvement over traditional methods. Our proposed method has the potential to be applied to a wide range of neural activity equations and could also be extended to other moment-based equations. This paper introduces a new approach to network reduction, referred to as network trimming through resource redistribution. The goal of network reduction, in general, is to minimize the combined cost of a transportation network by eliminating unnecessary edges, under the condition that the overall capacity remains unchanged. A key distinction of our method lies in its ability to redistribute any amount of capacity among edges, rather than strictly maintaining it. We formulate the problem as a mixed integer linear program and demonstrate its applicability in solving traditional network reduction problems when only a single resource is involved, ultimately leading to more efficient solutions. We further extend our approach to account for multiple resources and their impact on network reduction, highlighting its potential to inspire new research avenues and practical applications. The proposed method is exemplified through its implementation using a real-world case study involving the Romanian road network. We also provide a comprehensive computational complexity analysis of our network trimming technique. Ultimately, our network trimming through resource redistribution serves as a versatile tool for analyzing and optimizing various network-related problems. We envision that its findings will contribute to the advancement of network reduction research and its various practical applications. This paper introduces a novel, straightforward deep learning approach for processing 3D point clouds, which utilizes a standard point representation. By applying a simple positional encoding to points in the 3D point cloud, the network can be trained using widely available, pre-trained models from other fields such as image processing and 3D modeling. This approach, dubbed ParaNet, offers a simple and efficient solution for tasks like point cloud classification, segmentation, and pose estimation. Our experiments demonstrate that ParaNet achieves competitive results in these tasks while maintaining a level of interpretability that is unmatched by other deep learning methods. Furthermore, the network can be easily adapted to accommodate varying input sizes and can be trained using a small dataset, making it a highly efficient solution for point cloud analysis. The proliferation of machine learning has led to a growing preference for local training on individual devices, rather than central training, due to concerns about data privacy. Specifically, federated learning allows model training to occur on local devices while aggregating weights in a centralized server, without directly accessing local data. However, current FL approaches often overlook the unequal distribution of computational resources and privacy risks among participants. This disparity can result in biased models and unfair distribution of privacy risks, leading to poor performance. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework that promotes fairness in FL by accounting for individual contributions to the training process. This framework incorporates a new metric, called the fairness score, which assesses participant fairness based on their performance relative to the group. By using this score to inform updates, our approach aims to enhance the fairness of FL. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, which outperforms existing methods in terms of fairness and accuracy on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Additionally, our approach is compatible with various optimization algorithms and can be applied to diverse machine learning tasks, including classification and clustering. The way people perceive and process visual information is deeply influenced by the context in which they receive it, including time constraints. This study explores the effect of imposing a time limit on people's ability to analyze images. We conducted two separate experiments, one with 30 and the other with 30-minute time limits, to see how people's responses to the same set of images would change. The results showed that when given more time, people's answers became more accurate and consistent, but their focus shifted from the overall content of the image to its individual elements. To investigate this further, we looked into the role of image shapes in photo analysis and found that shapes played a significant part even under the stricter time constraint. However, the difference in image content prioritization between the two time limits was particularly noticeable in certain types of images, with 30-minute limit leading to more accurate results for objects and 30-second limit doing the same for overall image content. This discovery has significant implications for various fields, including image analysis, cybersecurity, and medical diagnosis, where image content interpretation is crucial. This finding also opens up possibilities for adjusting photo examination to suit different needs and contexts. To verify our findings, we also conducted a separate experiment where participants were asked to analyze the same set of images under both time constraints and were instructed to focus on different aspects. The results showed that when instructed to focus on shapes, people's answers became more accurate and consistent under the 30-second time limit, but not under the 30-minute limit, indicating that shapes indeed play a vital role in photo analysis. This research explores the connection between citizens' interactions and their political stance. We created a platform that connects users to two random fellow citizens for a discussion, and found that such discussions can be the cause of people shifting their views. However, this effect is influenced by how similar or opposed in opinion users are when matched initially. Our results show no change in opinion when discussing with someone who shares their views. Conversely, discussing with someone who strongly disagrees with them often leads to no change in opinion as well. Yet, when opposing views are moderate, there's a higher chance the discussing parties will ultimately agree. We discovered that such moderate disagreements lead to 'echo chambers' where users who hold opposing views are more likely to maintain or adopt those opposing views. Our findings were validated through both a controlled experiment and a large-scale analysis of a discussion forum. This research sheds light on the potential of discussing with those who have differing views. It also suggests that our current social media platforms may inadvertently restrict exposure to diverse viewpoints, which could be the result of a deliberate choice or an accidental byproduct. We propose that this issue could be addressed by incorporating features that encourage users to engage with opposing views. Our research provides insight into the complexities of human behavior and the intricacies of social media. It also offers a framework that can be used to study how social media shape our political views. Ultimately, this research aims to help us better understand the workings of democracy and how social media can either hinder or support it. In the realm of online optimization, we develop two novel adaptive search algorithms. The first algorithm, referred to as the Assist Cuckoo Search (ACS), utilizes a probabilistic approach where sub-nominal solutions are augmented by super-nominal solutions. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis of its convergence rate, which is found to be O(T^(1+1/n)) for T iterations. Building upon ACS, we introduce the second algorithm, referred to as the Adaptive Cuckoo Screens (ACSS), which dynamically adjusts the number of search spaces examined. By incorporating this adaptive mechanism, ACSS achieves a convergence rate of O((log T)^(1+1/n)). Our theoretical findings are substantiated through a comparative experimental evaluation involving standard algorithms like Cuckoo Search (CS) and its variants, Assist CS (ACS) and Adaptive Cuckoo Screens (ACSS). The experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed algorithms over their predecessors in terms of both efficiency and reliability. By using our newly designed complex number-based neural networks, which put the representation into the real part and imaginary part of the output, we achieved state-of-the-art results in various tasks, including handwritten recognition, speech recognition, and image recognition. This approach is flexible and can be applied to different types of neural networks, leading to enhanced performance and better understanding of the underlying mathematical principles. Furthermore, our work highlights the importance of using complex numbers in deep learning and provides a foundation for future research in this area. Our experiments revealed that a logistic regression model using MFCC-gram features and transformer attention weights achieved the best results, with an accuracy of 0.87 and an area under the curve of 0.87. Our method is underpinned by a new theoretical framework that enables the construction of GNNs from functors in an appropriate graph category. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this framework encompasses the Blaisbrock approach and introduce techniques for enhancing the expressiveness of our network through the incorporation of additional functorial terms. Our approach is also extendable to multi-graph settings and various other functor-based frameworks. Moreover, we provide a unified understanding of the Blaisbrock approach by relating it to the category-theoretic framework. Our work is further supported by experiments on real-world datasets, which validate the efficacy of our method in processing large-scale networks. Deep reinforcement learning agents may develop undesirable behaviors when their reward estimations contain errors, potentially leading to catastrophic failures. Despite this understanding, the relationship between reward estimation mistakes and undesirable behaviors remains unclear, and current research focuses primarily on mitigating these issues without fully grasping their root causes. This study investigates the connection between reward estimation mistakes and undesirable behaviors in RL agents, providing a framework to analyze this relationship. By employing this framework, we demonstrate that RL agents' undesirable behaviors can be attributed to two distinct issues: underestimating and overestimating rewards. Moreover, we propose a straightforward yet effective method to alleviate reward estimation mistakes, which we call "reward correction," and experimentally verify its effectiveness in mitigating undesirable behaviors. These findings provide valuable insights into mitigating undesirable behaviors in RL agents and offer a foundation for future research on this topic. The primary objective of designing learned indexes is to minimize the time required for a query to return relevant results.  A learned index can be viewed as a two-part system, consisting of a search function and a data storage component.  The search function determines which data segments may contain the desired information, and the data storage component is responsible for retrieving the actual data.  This paper examines the feasibility of using neural networks to develop the search function, with the data storage component remaining non-neural and based on established data structures.  The study involves comparing neural and non-neural search functions in various configurations, with the data storage component kept constant across all experiments.  The results indicate that using a neural network for the search function can lead to significant performance improvements, with some setups delivering a 50% reduction in query time.  However, the data storage component plays a crucial role in this improvement, with optimal data structure selection being essential for achieving the best neural network-based performance outcomes.  The findings also suggest that neural network-based search functions can be successfully trained on data consisting of only a few examples, with some configurations demonstrating comparable efficiency on a dataset containing 10 records as on a dataset containing 100 records.  This study's results are expected to provide valuable guidance for designing learned indexes that offer improved performance compared to traditional data structures. A novel approach to assessing the energy performance of RC shear walls has been developed using a combination of finite element analysis and machine learning techniques. This approach first utilizes a nonlinear FE model to simulate the behavior of the walls under various load conditions, generating a database that includes key structural and damage metrics. This database is then used to train a deep neural network that can predict the damage extent to the structural members for new, unseen load combinations. The proposed method enables the estimation of critical structural damage using a simplified, two-hour seismic analysis, thereby facilitating the development of energy performance charts that can help owners assess the severity of seismic damage and make informed decisions regarding repair, replace, or retain decisions. The effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through its application to a benchmark problem and a real-world case study involving a building with multiple seismic hazard levels. The results indicate that the deep learning model can accurately predict the damage extent to the structural members and estimate energy demand with a high degree of accuracy. The use of the proposed method can significantly reduce the computational cost associated with energy performance assessments, enabling rapid analysis of multiple building scenarios and facilitating more efficient and effective decision-making processes. The authors believe that this research has the potential to revolutionize the practice of seismic assessment and design by providing a rapid, cost-effective, and efficient framework for energy performance evaluations. Our research is the first to explore retraining in reinforcement learning as a viable solution for dynamic settings. In a scenario where multiple experts collaborate on a private forecasting problem, we examine how their individual price schedules impact the resulting mechanism. We demonstrate that any pricing strategy can be mapped to an equivalent single-valued cost function, which we refer to as the equivalent cost, and derive a key relationship: the sum of the equivalent costs for optimal pricing matches the social cost of the optimal mechanism. This finding is versatile enough to apply to various social welfare measures and provides insight into the existing literature on private forecasting, highlighting its connection to the mechanism design paradigm. We also illustrate that, in general, no optimal mechanism can be constructed when experts' costs are non-linear, posing a significant challenge. This prompts us to propose a novel class of mechanisms, the polynomial scoring rules, which ensure a linear approximation of the social welfare measure. We establish that these mechanisms achieve a near-optimal approximation for a private forecasting problem involving a single expert, and extend this result to multiple experts with a polynomial equivalent cost, showing that these mechanisms closely approximate the optimal solution. We also establish a lower bound on the approximation ratio for polynomial scoring mechanisms, demonstrating that they are near-optimal for a given class of private forecasting problems. This research introduces a novel method for evaluating correlations from data that has been censored, leveraging the characteristics of the Tobit model. Building upon the original work of Keng-Sheng Kuo, et al. (2016), who utilized multiple point estimates to derive correlation measures, we first extend their methodology to accommodate the estimation of mean and median under an uneven censored data scenario. The Go programming language has become a preferred choice for creating concurrent software due to its unique blend of simplicity and effectiveness. As a result of its widespread adoption, there is a pressing need for reliable methods to detect and verify concurrency issues within Go programs. Unfortunately, Go's simplicity and lack of formal concurrency verification features make it challenging to apply traditional verification techniques. In response to this problem, we introduce BinGo, a novel tool that leverages static binary analysis to identify concurrency problems in Go programs. BinGo's approach involves analyzing the intermediate code produced by the Go compiler to detect potential issues, including runtime errors, synchronization hazards, and race conditions. Our evaluation of BinGo involved testing it on a diverse set of Go programs, including those used in cloud-based applications, and demonstrated its ability to identify known and unknown concurrency issues in real-world packages. Furthermore, we applied BinGo to a set of popular Go frameworks and libraries, resulting in the detection of several hundred potential concurrency issues. These findings highlight the effectiveness of BinGo and underscore the need for more robust methods to verify the reliability of Go programs in the context of large-scale, concurrent systems. This paper introduces a novel reinforcement learning approach that merges the strengths of model-free value function estimation and model-based policy generation through modular MPC, ultimately resulting in a more efficient learning process. The development of highly accurate deep learning models is hindered by the significant time and computational resources required.  Models that have already been trained can be leveraged to accelerate the training of new models, a process known as model knowledge or checkpoint knowledge transfer.  This method involves utilizing the pre-existing knowledge from an initial model to jumpstart the training of a secondary model, with the ultimate goal of achieving higher performance.  This paper undertakes an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness of model-based knowledge transfer across various neural network architectures, including CNNs, VGG, ResNet, and DenseNet, with a focus on image classification tasks.  The findings reveal that the choice of model architecture and training parameters has a substantial impact on the success of model-based knowledge transfer.  Specifically, VGG models tend to outperform ResNet and DenseNet models in terms of accuracy, while VGG and ResNet models exhibit greater stability in the training process.  Furthermore, the study examines the influence of the number of transferred layers and the stopping criteria on the effectiveness of model-based knowledge transfer.  The results demonstrate that the transfer of a limited number of layers (e.g., 50-60%) is sufficient to achieve optimal performance, with early stopping criteria also contributing to enhanced model accuracy.  The findings of this study are expected to facilitate the development of more efficient model-based knowledge transfer methods and improve the design of deep learning models.  The accompanying code can be accessed at the GitHub repository https://github.com/rahulsharish/Model-Checkpoint-Knowledge-Transfer. We introduce a novel approach to extracting features from data using a neural network, where the goal is to identify a set of random features that capture the underlying data patterns. Our method, called MetaKernel, leverages this network to produce a set of variational features that maximize a chosen kernel similarity score. MetaKernel stands out from existing random feature approximation techniques by: (i) providing a non-parametric framework for learning data patterns, (ii) offering a probabilistic model of the data, and (iii) enabling the learning of data patterns across multiple kernels. In order to facilitate practical applications, we propose a kernel-based classifier that can be trained with a limited number of labeled examples, even when the labeled data is scarce. MetaKernel's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on various datasets, showcasing its ability to outperform established methods in terms of generalization performance. Our implementation is publicly available on GitHub. For instance, on the dataset of 3D shapes, MetaKernel achieves a 2% improvement in classification accuracy compared to a fully supervised SVM. Furthermore, on the dataset of protein sequences, MetaKernel achieves a 5% improvement in classification accuracy at 10% labeled data, outperforming existing random feature approximation methods. Our approach also shows promising results in semi-supervised learning settings. Our work provides a new direction for the development of kernel-based learning methods that can be applied to a wide range of domains. SLAM has become a crucial component in the development of autonomous systems, particularly in robotics and augmented reality. The integration of SLAM and visual SLAM holds significant promise for enhancing augmented reality capabilities. Visual SLAM, which relies on images to track motion, offers several advantages, including compactness and real-time performance, but is susceptible to significant errors in long-term positioning accuracy. To address this issue, we introduce a novel SLAM approach that combines the global positioning precision of visual SLAM with the global consistency of feature-based SLAM. The proposed method achieves this by representing the scene as a network of interconnected features, which are simultaneously tracked and viewed during movement. The scene's topological structure is reconstructed from the resulting feature relationships, enabling the global optimization of feature connections and reducing the accumulation of errors over time. The reserve supply in an electricity market is crucial to ensure supply security, yet managing its size is complex due to uncertainties like weather and demand. This research proposes a data-driven approach to dynamically adjust reserve levels based on forecasted probabilities of grid disruptions. By analyzing historical data on grid disruptions and their causes, the method calculates the likelihood of specific disruptions occurring and sizes reserves accordingly. Simulation results show that this adaptive reserve management strategy outperforms fixed-sized approaches and traditional data-driven methods, achieving better cost-effectiveness and supply security. Notably, the method demonstrates significant cost savings while maintaining supply security. This research provides a valuable framework for optimizing reserve management using real-world data and probabilistic forecasts. Further applications of this approach could lead to enhanced supply security and economic performance in electricity markets.

A new statistical method for partial least squares regression has been developed,
which utilizes IV analysis to analyze non-linear relationships in high-dimensional
datasets. This approach, called Profound PLS, is an expectation-maximization based
algorithm that iteratively updates regression and prediction parameters to achieve
optimal solutions. Empirical studies have demonstrated that Profound PLS outperforms
traditional PLS regression, especially when dealing with complex non-linear data,
resulting in more reliable model predictions and improved robustness to noise.
Furthermore, Profound PLS has been shown to be computationally efficient, capable of
handling large datasets in a relatively short timeframe, making it a promising tool
for handling high-dimensional datasets in fields like bioinformatics and machine
learning. In this context, Profound PLS has been successfully applied to a
gene-expression dataset to analyze the non-linear relationships between gene
expression levels and breast cancer phenotypes. The results indicate that Profound PLS
can accurately predict breast cancer phenotypes using gene expression data, even in
cases where the data exhibits non-linear patterns, and that the method is capable of
withstanding variations in feature selection, which can lead to improved model
robustness. Overall, Profound PLS has been found to be a reliable and efficient
approach for analyzing high-dimensional data, especially in the presence of
non-linear relationships. In addition, Profound PLS has been found to be a valuable
tool for identifying key variables in bioinformatics and machine learning applications. The Profound PLS algorithm is available as an open-source R package. The widespread use of Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) has made it an essential component in modern computer networks. However, the lack of transparency in MPLS networks has hindered the development of monitoring and analysis tools. To address this issue, we propose TNT, a network monitoring system that utilizes traffic analysis to identify and uncover MPLS tunnels. TNT leverages machine learning techniques to accurately map and map multiple layers of MPLS networks. Our findings demonstrate TNT's effectiveness in uncovering 95% of MPLS tunnels and achieving high accuracy. Furthermore, our results show that TNT significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving a 94.7% true positive rate and minimizing false positives. Notably, our study is the first to uncover Tier-2 MPLS networks, revealing a substantial number of hidden tunnels. The source code for TNT is available online for academic and research purposes. Our research aims to facilitate the development of more sophisticated monitoring and analysis tools, enabling network operators to gain a deeper understanding of MPLS networks. By doing so, we hope to shed light on the intricacies of these complex systems.

Extracting structured data from unorganized text has been a long-standing challenge for artificial intelligence.  Addressing this challenge, open information extraction systems aim to automatically identify and collect facts from online content without preconceived notions.  Current open information extraction systems, although effective, have significant limitations, primarily due to their inability to tie contextual information to the facts they extract.  This results in a lack of understanding of the specific setting in which a fact was extracted, ultimately limiting their practical utility.  To overcome these constraints, we introduce Graphene, an innovative system that utilizes a graph-based approach to connect extracted facts with their corresponding contexts.  This graph structure enables Graphene to effectively capture the full context of the fact, including the specific words surrounding it and the sentences in which they are expressed.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted a thorough evaluation of Graphene's performance on three public open information extraction benchmarks, resulting in superior performance compared to existing systems, with the added benefit of context preservation.  To facilitate further research, the Graphene system and accompanying data will be made publicly available.  A video demonstration of this method can be found at https://youtu.be/6s8s5qzKQ8A. This paper delves into compact specialization of runtime settings, a technique that optimizes programs by eliminating unnecessary runtime computations. By moving the calculation of variable assignments from runtime to compile-time, it reduces the runtime footprint. We apply this concept to a simple language, introducing a compile-time algorithm that specializes variable assignments. Through experimental evaluation, we demonstrate the effectiveness of compile-time specialization in terms of precision and efficiency. By comparing the outcomes against a reference specialization performed at runtime, we highlight the benefits of compile-time specialization in terms of precision, size, and execution speed. Furthermore, our results indicate that a substantial portion of variable assignments can be specialized at compile-time, resulting in a considerable reduction in size. We also provide recommendations for integrating this specialization technique into real-world languages. The accompanying source code is available on GitHub.

This study aims to analyze and categorize code odors detection techniques in research by identifying relevant studies, observing patterns, and providing guidance on selecting appropriate methods for specific contexts. We conducted a systematic review of 85 studies from 2011 to 2020, which revealed that 43 different code odors detection methods have been proposed. Our analysis shows that most studies focus on detecting code odors in individual systems, while only a few use machine learning techniques. Furthermore, we found that code odors detection methods can be grouped into three main categories: system analysis, team collaboration, and technical implementation. While our study's findings are a valuable contribution to the field, they also highlight several limitations, including the lack of standard code odors classification and the need for more research in this area. Future research could benefit from integrating multiple code odors detection methods to provide more accurate results and exploring the use of machine learning techniques to detect code odors. The thermal stability of fluid in Rayleigh-Benard convection is examined by analyzing the marginally-stable thermal balance, which is achieved when the growth rate of temperature fluctuations approaches zero. This condition is characterized by a self-sustaining mechanism that maintains thermal equilibrium. Through a perturbation analysis, the thermal balance is derived from the fully nonlinear equations governing convection, assuming a marginally-stable state. This thermal balance is then compared to that obtained from the linearized eigenvalue problem, which is characterized by a Rayleigh number, to gain insights into the convection dynamics. This thermal balance is a useful tool for understanding the dynamics of convection and for predicting the onset of instability in turbulent flows. A novel approach for estimating rock permeability from 3D micro-CT images is introduced, utilizing a physics-informed convolutional neural network. This framework is grounded in the Navier-Stokes equations and incorporates a novel loss function based on the absolute flux differences between simulated and predicted flow fields. Our method demonstrates high accuracy in permeability estimation, particularly for porous media with moderate to high permeability, according to comparisons with historical data. However, for rocks with low permeability, the predicted results are overestimated, suggesting that the physical constraints of the physics-informed network are overly influenced by the low-permeability rocks' smooth flow field. This approach has potential applications in estimating rock properties from 3D images. All underlying code is available on GitHub. As video conferencing continues to evolve, the need for high-quality video transmission has become more pressing, necessitating increased bandwidth and lower latency, despite the constraints of wireless networks and shifting priorities. To address this issue, our innovative video compression system, Gemino, utilizes a unique combination of lossy and lossless compression methods to prioritize high-quality face and upper body content, including video, audio, and control signals. By incorporating a novel low-cost fractal-based image compressor and a real-time, low-latency video decoder, Gemino achieves substantial bandwidth reductions, specifically a 10:1 to 20:1 reduction with only 0.5% perceived quality loss, while maintaining real-time performance and outperforming existing solutions by 30%. Additionally, the system's resilience to packet loss has been successfully demonstrated, enabling seamless operation even in the presence of high loss rates. Our results also show that Gemino's performance remains effective in various real-world scenarios, including dynamic camera motion and changing network conditions. By addressing the critical issues of bandwidth and latency, Gemino represents a significant step towards making high-quality video conferencing a reality over wireless networks. This research has been made available as an open-source software package for further development and use. Furthermore, our study highlights the potential of using fractal-based image compression to improve the efficiency of other applications, such as video editing and generation, and to explore new avenues in the field of computer vision. By pioneering the use of fractal-based image compression in video conferencing, Gemino has opened up new possibilities for this and related fields. Our work has been recognized with an award at the 2022 ACM Conference on Data and Text Engineering. To facilitate the adoption of Gemino, we have developed a practical guide for its implementation and deployment. The Gravity Spy program utilizes the Advanced LIGO detectors' public waveforms from their first and second data collection phases to develop a classification system for transient events. This program's main objective is to identify and eliminate instrumental noise from the collected astrophysical signals, ensuring the data's integrity. By applying machine learning techniques to audio-like representations of the waveforms, the Gravity Spy system categorizes these events into distinct groups. In this paper, the classification system's development and application to the second data collection phase are discussed. Additionally, the study examines the performance of the classification system in relation to the first data collection phase and makes recommendations for future improvements. Furthermore, the research investigates the relationship between waveform characteristics and their classification labels, providing a deeper understanding of the LIGO detectors' behavior during the different data collection phases. The findings suggest that the classification system's accuracy has improved in the second data collection phase, particularly in identifying glitches. Moreover, the study reveals that the classification labels are associated with distinct noise sources and methods used to analyze them. The research also provides a detailed analysis of the classification performance, comparing it to the first data collection phase and discussing the implications of the classification system's limitations. The study's results are made publicly available through an interactive data visualization tool. The Gravity Spy system's continued development and refinement are also discussed, with a focus on incorporating new features and improving the classification accuracy. The research highlights the potential of the classification system to detect previously unknown noise sources and improve the data integrity of the LIGO detectors. The study's results are expected to contribute to the development of more effective noise identification and removal methods for future LIGO data collection phases.
